previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with brittle type 1 diabetes, recurrent gastroparesis, chronic kidney disease stage II, and a history of anxiety and depression was readmitted within 24 hours of discharge due to persistent abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting, consistent with a gastroparesis flare. Her symptoms were exacerbated by uncontrolled diabetes and possible gastroesophageal reflux. Chest tightness was evaluated with a normal chest X-ray, ruling out acute cardiopulmonary causes. She was managed with IV fluids, insulin adjustment to her home NPH regimen, and anti-nausea medications while avoiding contraindicated drugs due to allergies. She gradually advanced to a soft diet, with improvement in symptoms and stable renal function. Omeprazole was continued for acid suppression. A coordinated discharge plan included follow-up with her primary care provider, mental health support, and ophthalmology for background diabetic retinopathy. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions for ongoing diabetes and gastroparesis management.

================
ACTIVE PROBLEMS:
================
# Gastroparesis flare: Likely related to known gastroparesis, 
with symptoms similar to prior gastroparesis flares. Unclear 
reason for acute worsening of her gastroparesis, but likely due 
to hyperglycemia. Her abominal pain improved during the 
admission, nausea and vomiting resolved, and she was able to 
take medications and food by mouth.  She was advised that 
narcotics and hyperglycemia can worsen gastroparesis, which she 
was already aware.  Because the patient had previously had a 
sub-optimal gastric emptying study while on narcotics, the 
emptying study was repeated.  The patient was able to refrain 
from narcotics, zofran, and laxatives for almost 48 hours prior 
to the exam, with the exception of one dose oxycodone that was 
taken 16 hours prior to the study.  The exam was still 
sub-optimal as the patient was on metoclopramide and still had 
poor glycemic control, but confirmed delayed gastric emptying at 
2, 3, and 4 hours. She was again educated and understood that 
she should eat smaller more frequent meals as well as avoiding 
narcotics to help control her symptoms.

# Hyperglycemia/T1DM: Hyperglycemia may have occurred in the 
setting of medication non-compliance, as the patient reported 
not taking recommended insulin doses in the setting of poor 
intake, because she was afraid of hypoglycemic episodes. She did 
not have evidence of DKA on admission.  ___ was 
consulted for adjustement of insulin regimen, and changed her 
QHS lantus to 14U (from 10U).  Her sliding scale and AM dose of 
lantus (6U) remained unchanged.  At the time she left the 
hospital her sugars were still poorly controlled (generally 
ranging between 200-450). She wished to return home to her son 
prior to having her FSBGs under better control. She understood 
the risks of her decision and follow up with ___ was arranged 
the day after discharge.  

# Hypertensive urgency: At the time of admission the patient was 
hypertensive with systolic blood pressures in the 200s, but was 
asymptomatic.  She was started on her home furosemide, 
labetalol, and amlodipine, and blood pressures improved and 
remained in the 130s-150s for the remainder of her admission. 
Her hypertension was most likely secondary to noncompliance as 
restarting her home medications improved her pressures.

# Difficult Access: The patient was scheduled for port placement 
prior to this hospitalization, and the decision was made to try 
to have port placed during this admission because of difficulty 
maintaining good IV access.  The patient decided to leave prior 
to port placement, so a plan was made for port placement in the 
outpatient setting.

# Pseudohyponatremia: Sodium 128 on admission but corrected 
sodium 138. This improved during her admission with better 
glycemic control.

===================

V chronic kidney disease and is on dialysis ___.  She 
continued on this dialysis schedule while in the hospital.  Her 
last dialysis session was delayed in order to obtain the gastric 
emptying study.  She was continued on nephrocaps and sevelamer. 
PTH was checked and >600, so she was started on vitamin D and 
calcium.

# Back Pain: Patient has chronic back pain following a motor 
vehicle accident and take percocet at home.  She was continued 
on her home pain regimen except prior to her gastric emptying 
study, when she was encouraged to use alternative means of pain 
control (tylenol, lidocaine patch).
s/p MVA

# Anemia: Patient has anemia likely secondary to chronic disease 
and decreased erythropoetin production.  Her anemia was at her 
baseline from prior admission and remained similar.

with coping skills.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you while you were at ___.

You were admitted because you were having severe abdominal pain 
with nausea and vomiting at home as well as very high blood 
sugars.  This is a problem that you have had many times and 
likely represents worsening of your gastroparesis (poor stomach 
emptying) from your diabetes.  As you know, many things can 
worsen your problems with gastric emptying including having high 
blood sugar as well as certain medications (narcotics, zofran). 
You were continued on Reglan (medication to help with stomach 
emptying) and given pain medications to help with your acute 
abdominal pain.  Your pain improved while you were admitted and 
you were able to start eating again without further vomiting.  
We had you get a gastric emptying study to evaluate your 
gastroparesis, and the results of this study are still pending 
and will need follow up. We had you avoid taking narcotics and 
other medications that interfere with the results of this study.

You also had high blood sugars, with at blood sugar of more than 
700 when you were admitted.  The diabetes team saw you and made 
adjustments to your insulin medication doses.  Your sugars 
improved but not as much as we would like. You wanted to be 
discharged with high blood sugars still because you wanted to 
take care of your son. You understood the risks of leaving the 
hospital with high blood sugars. We would like for you to be 
seen in the ___ Diabetes clinic so that they can adjust your 
insulin once you are at home.  The high sugar levels can also 
worsen your problems with abdominal pain and poor stomach 
emptying.

You continued your usual dialysis and medications for your 
kidney failure while you were in the hospital.  We checked a 
hormone called PTH (parathyroid) which becomes elevated when you 
have kidney failure, and because it was high we started you on 
Vitamin D with calcium.  You should continue this medication at 
home.
  
We spoke with your kidney doctor, ___ agreed with 
our plan to place a port for better intravenous access (to give 
medications by IVs and draw blood).  However, your port 
placement was delayed before your were discharged.  You will 
need to arrange to come in to the hospital to get the port 
placed at another time.

At the end of your stay here, your medical team felt that you 
should stay to improve your blood sugar control.  You felt that 
your abdominal pain had improved and that you no longer wanted 
to stay in the hospital.  We explained that your sugars were not 
well controlled and that it was our medical opinion that you 
were not ready to leave the hospital.  You expressed 
understanding of our medical advice, and wished to be 
discharged.  We have set up a follow up appointment for you to 
be seen at ___ tomorrow ___.

We wish you all the best,
Your ___ Team
